list.listitem: Any patient with aphasia/focal neurological defect should be considered for stroke diagnosis.C
Urgent CT or MRI should be ordered to distinguish between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke.A
Intracranial pressure (ICP) should be promptly lowered if abnormal (see ).B
If present, anticoagulant drugs should be counteracted.B

Emergent minimally invasive surgical evacuation is recommended for patients with larger hemorrages (>15 mL), when there is evidence of neurological deterioration, brainstem compression, or hydrocephalus.B
The patient should be referred to a stroke unit if available.B

background.definition: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is an acute extravasation of blood into the brain parenchyma. ICH commonly occur in the cerebral lobes (lobar ICH) or in basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem and cerebellum (nonlobar ICH).

list.listitem: Worldwide: 0.01 to 0.02 per 1000 persons per year
Among African-Americans: >0.05 per 1000 persons per year, and in Japanese population 0.055 per 1000 persons per year

More common as patients get older: 0.011 per 1000 persons per year <55 years: 2 per 1000 per year at age 55 to 64, 7 per 1000 per year at age 65 to 74, 14 per 1000 per year at age 75 to 84, and 25 per 1000 per year over age 85 years
37,000 to 52,000 new cases each year in the USA
Hypertensive arteriolosclerosis
Amyloid angiopathy
Trauma
Arteriovenous malformation
Anticoagulants (rivaroxaban with higher bleeding risk than apixaban)
Intracranial aneurysm
Coagulopathy
Hemorrhagic conversion of cerebral infarction
Dural sinus thrombosis
Intracranial neoplasm
Cavernous angioma
Venous angioma
Cocaine or sympathomimetic drug exposure
Vasculitis of the CNS
Monoclonal antibodies targetting amyloid and tau proteins.
IV thrombolytics.
ICH results from the rupture of the small penetrating arteries that originate from basilar arteries or the anterior, middle, or posterior cerebral arteries.
Degenerative changes in the vessel wall induced by chronic hypertension or amyloid angiopathy reduce compliance and increase the likelihood of spontaneous rupture.

The hematoma expands over time. Continued bleeding from the primary source has been attributed to this expansion along with the mechanical disruption of surrounding vessels. Acute hypertension, a local coagulation deficit, or both may be associated with expansion of the hematoma.
The presence of hematoma initiates edema and neuronal damage in surrounding parenchyma.
Blood pressure lowering to normal values is the mainstay of primary and secondary prevention of ICH, although rapid reduction may worsen neurologic outcomes.A
Patients should be advised to stop smoking, avoid heavy alcohol use, and abstain from cocaine use.B
In patients with a clinical indication for oral anticoagulation (eg, atrial fibrillation) who survive an ICH, carefully consider switching to aspirin or no treatment at all.B
Consider stroke, including ICH, in any patient with aphasia or focal neurological deficit.C
CT and MRI are each first-choice initial imaging options.A
ICH is a medical emergency, with frequent early ongoing bleeding, and it has to be rapidly suspected and diagnosed.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Focal deficit; negative brain imaging at onset or ischemia
Negative brain imaging; lone memory deficit
Absence of focal deficit; aura; negative brain imaging or causative lesion
Clinically indistinguishable; plain CT scan suggestive; contrast CT or MRI diagnostic

Differential.Differential_Name: Metabolic coma (diabetes, alcohol abuse, hypernatremia, overdose)
Differential.Differential_Features: Focal deficit and hemisyndrome usually absent; negative brain imaging

list.listitem: Patients typically present with a rapid onset of focal neurological deficits. Headache is more common in subarachnoid hemorrhage than in intraparenchymal hemorrhage or ischemic stroke. Other features suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage include loss of consciousness or complaints of neck stiffness confirmed on exam.
Supratentorial ICH: contralateral motor or sensorial deficits, aphasia, neglect, gaze deviation, hemianopsia.
Infratentorial ICH: abnormalities of gaze, cranial nerve abnormalities, contralateral motor deficit, ataxia, nystagmus, and dysmetria.
Clinical signs of high ICP include abrupt change in level of consciousness, headache, and vomiting.
Epileptic seizures might occur at onset or more commonly weeks to year after.

Plain CT and MRI are each first-choice initial imaging options.Plain CT and MRI offers complementary information and both should routinely be planned; CT alone should be obtained in patients with contraindication to MRI.
CT without contrast is the recommended initial imaging study to rule out hemorrhage in the emergency settings.
If contrast CT is to be performed, consider CT perfusion. CT angiography has good diagnostic accuracy relative to digital subtraction angiography.
MRI (no contrast, diffusion weighted) has higher resolution for ischemia and identifies even small and early lesions.
MRI (with contrast) is indicated if vascular lesion/malformation is suspected.
Patients with putaminal, thalamic, or cerebellar hemorrhage should undergo conventional angiography if they are below 45 years and normotensive.

Two clinical decision rules have been developed and validated to predict the likelihood of hemorrhagic vs nonhemorrhagic infarct. The first, by Efstathiou and colleagues, uses recent neurological deterioration, vomiting, elevated WBC, and decreased level of consciousness to predict hemorrhage. A second rule by Besson and colleagues has also been prospectively validated.
Clinical decision rules to predict the likelihood of intracranial hemorrhage in patients undergoing thrombolysis for acute stroke are moderately accurate.

Confirm the presence of a recent onset acute focal neurological deficit, including loss of speech, unilateral weakness or paresthesias in an extremity or face, visual field loss, vertigo associated with other cranial nerve abnormalities (eg, double-vision, gaze, deviation, difficulty speaking, imbalance).

It is difficult to reliably distinguish hemorrhagic from ischemic strokes, even using validated decision rules. Even patients being treated with anticoagulants, ischemic, and hemorrhagic stroke have a similar probability.
Perform cranial CT or MRI within 30 minutes of presentation, if possible.
Treat elevated ICP (eg, mannitol 20%, 100 mL q4h for 5 days then tapered over 2 days).B
Reduce blood pressure, guided by initial blood pressure and presence or absence of increased ICP ().C
If the patient is on vitamin K antagonists, reverse anticoagulation (eg, vitamin K, FFP, PCC, rFVIIa).B

Emergent minimally invasive surgical evacuation is recommended for patients with larger hemorrages (>15 mL), when there is evidence of neurological deterioration, brainstem compression, or hydrocephalus.B
Refer patients to a dedicated stroke unit if available.C
No specific drug treatment is available to stop ongoing bleeding in the patients with normal coagulation.
Rapidly reverse coagulopathy in patients taking anticoagulants (eg, protamine sulfate for heparin, IV vitamin K for warfarin). Consider using prothrombin complex concentrates or fresh frozen plasma..

Patients taking Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and fondaparinux) represent a challenge to reversal of anticoagulation. A study randomized 530 patients with acute intracerebral hemorrhage to andaxanet (a modified, inactive form of factor Xa that inactivates Factor Xa inhibitors) or placebo. The primary outcome was hemostatic efficacy at 12 hours, defined as an increase in the hematoma volume of less than or equal 35%, an increase in the NIHSS score of no more than 7 points, and no need for rescue therapy or surgery. This outcome occurred significantly more often with andexanet (67% vs 53%, NNT = 8). However, there were more ischemic strokes (6.4% vs 1.5%) and MIs (4.2% vs 1.5%) in the andaxanet group, no difference in all cause mortality, and no difference in the number with a modified Rankin score of 0 to 3.

Reduction in hematoma growth was shown for recombinant factor VIIa, but a subsequent confirmatory trial failed to show advantage in terms of survival. A recent Cochrane review concluded that current evidence for the use of hemostatic drugs (eg, factor VIIa) in the treatment of ICH is inadequate to guide clinical practice.
Treat elevated ICP (eg, mannitol 20%, 100 mL q 4 hour for 5 days, then tapered over 2 days). Maintain cerebral perfusion pressure >70 mm Hg and constantly monitor ICP and blood pressure.

Good clinical trials regarding blood pressure control in patients with ICH are lacking. See for consensus recommendations. Antihypertensive options include labetalol (5-20 mg IV every 20 minutes, then 2 mg/min continuous IV infusion) or esmolol (250 mcg/kg IV push loading dose, then 25-300 mcg/kg/min continuous infusion). Early intensive lowering of blood pressure in ICH does not decrease mortality; evidence on functional outcomes is conflicting.
There is no evidence of an beneficial or adverse effect of corticosteroid treatment in patients with ICH.
Edaravone, an antioxidant, has been studied in ten randomized controlled trials among patients with acute ICH; evidence is inconclusive as to whether there is clinical benefit.

A trial randomized 319 patients with atrial fibrillation who had experienced an intracerebral hemorrhage to a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) or to no anticoagulant. In the DOAC group, the risk of stroke was lower (0.83 vs 8.70 per 100 person-years) but the risk of intracerebral hemorrhage was higher (5.0 vs 0.82 per 100 person-years).
ASA guidelines recommend against the use of prophylactic corticosteroids or continuous hyperosmolar therapy because of lack of evidence of effectiveness and potential harms.

The routine evacuation of supratentorial ICH by standard craniotomy within 96 hours of bleeding is not recommended by American Stroke Association guidelines (2022). Minimally invasive approaches to evacuate and intraventricular and supratentorial hemorrhages have been shown to reduce mortality with an uncertain impact on function.

Emergent minimally invasive surgical evacuation is recommended for patients with larger hemorrages (>15 mL), when there is evidence of neurological deterioration, brainstem compression, or hydrocephalus.

A trial randomized 300 patients with lobar or anterior basal ganglia hemorrhage (volume 30 to 80 ml) to guideline directed care or to guideline directed care plus minimally invasive surgical removal of the hematoma. Mortality was significantly lower in the surgery group (9.3% vs 18.0%) and for those with lobar hemorrhage (but not anterior basal ganglion hemorrhage) function at 6 months was also improved. These findings were consistent with those of a large registry-based study.
Encourage early mobilization as soon as the patient is stable.
Physical rehabilitation treatment and language rehabilitation treatment improve global functioning of the patient and should be started as soon as the patient is stable.
Nasogastric feeding is often recommended, but whether it reduces or increases risk of aspiration pneumonia is controversial.
Patients with Glasgow Coma Scale <8 at hospitalization should undergo emergency ventilation or mechanical intubation.
Other than in the setting of emergency surgery or in the patient with severe thrombocytopenia, use of platelet transfusions worsens outcomes and is not recommended by ASA guidelines (2022).
All patients should be referred and hospitalized.

Give appropriate antiepileptic drugs in patients with epileptic seizures; give intravenously if seizure at onset. Long-term treatment should be considered only if further seizures at least 2 weeks after the onset.
Treat sources of fever and use antipyretic medication in febrile patients.
Patients with acute primary ICH and hemiparesis/hemiplegia should have intermittent pneumatic compression for prevention of venous thromboembolism.B
Prophylactic doses of low molecular weight heparin or unfractionated heparin may be considered in hemiplegic patients beginning 3 to 4 days from onset.
If deep vein thrombosis is diagnosed, a vena cava filter should be placed.

Monitoring and management of patients with an ICH must take place in an ICU because of the acuity of the condition, frequent elevations in ICP and blood pressure, frequent need for intubation and assisted ventilation, and multiple complicating medical issues.
One-year mortality ranges from 42% to 65%.B
Permanent disability at 6 months in up to 80% of patients.B
Thirty-day mortality rate is 35% to 52%.
Fifty percent of deaths occur in the fist 2 days since symptoms onset.
One-year mortality ranges from 42% to 65%.
At 6 months, up to 80% of patients are permanently disabled.
Hematoma volume >30 mL, ventricular hemorrhage, cerebral edema, midline shift are also associated with a worse prognosis.
Patients on anticoagulants have a 2- to 3-fold increase in mortality; spontaneous events have a 1.5- to 3-fold increase in mortality.
Patients on dabigatran, a novel oral anticoagulant, were shown to have similar outcomes after a major bleeding episode when compared to subjects on warfarin.
Neurological scale scores (ie, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) correlate with prognosis.
Patients aged 18 to 50 years surviving ICH are in a cohort of patients (including those with TIA and ischemic stroke) with a higher than expected mortality rate compared to the standard population.
Small vessel disease on CT scan at the time of ICH diagnosis predicted poorer neurologic outcomes in one study.

feature.caption: Consensus Recommendation Based on Expert Opinion for Blood Pressure Control in Patients with Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
feature.feature_body:
Clinical Situation Intracranial Pressure (ICP) Recommendation
SBP >200 mm Hg or MAP >150 mm Hg
Consider aggressive reduction of blood pressure with continuous intravenous infusion, with frequent blood pressure monitoring every 5 minutes
SBP >180 mm Hg or MAP >130 mm Hg Evidence of, or suspicion of, elevated ICP Consider monitoring ICP and reducing blood pressure using intermittent or continuous IV medications to keep cerebral perfusion pressure >60-80 mm Hg
SBP >180 mm Hg or MAP >130 mm Hg No evidence or suspicion of elevated ICP Consider a modest reduction of blood pressure (eg, MAP = 110 mm Hg or target blood pressure = 160/90 mm Hg) using intermittent or continuous IV medications to control blood pressure, and clinically reexamine the patient every 15 minutes
SBP, systolic blood pressure; MAP, mean arterial blood pressure.
